decisions.title: The product supervises the human's attention, not the agents
decisions.why: This is client work: the decisions are the user's because the responsibility is, and an autonomous supervisor moves risk somewhere nobody looks.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It is a claim about what the product is for. No import boundary can tell a queue that ranks decisions from one that takes them.

alternatives.option: Supervisor–worker orchestration
alternatives.why_not: The dominant pattern in every agent framework, and what the comparable tools build. It removes the human from decisions the human wants to make.

alternatives.option: L3 autonomy, agents deciding for themselves
alternatives.why_not: The goal was never to decide less. It was to decide better, which is the opposite optimisation.

alternatives.option: Parallel panes with no supervision
alternatives.why_not: Keeps the human in the loop and helps them not at all. Prettier terminals, same cognitive load.

decisions.title: The product informs, you decide; nothing blocks
decisions.why: A product that dictates workflow gets worked around on the first urgent day, and then the information is lost along with the block.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: A rule can see that code exists, not that it refuses. Whether a check blocks or merely reports is behaviour, not shape.

alternatives.option: Blocking on unsatisfied preconditions
alternatives.why_not: False confidence, and it gets disabled. Whoever wants to bypass it opens a terminal.

alternatives.option: Hard limits on WIP, diff size or resources
alternatives.why_not: The same, plus it punishes legitimate work.

decisions.title: The workspace is the confidentiality boundary, not the machine
decisions.why: One runtime can host two workspaces and one workspace can span runtimes; treating them as a single axis is the most likely source of a leak.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: The boundary is a property of configuration at runtime, not of the import graph. What a rule *can* keep is the crate that carries no content, which ADR-004 owns.

alternatives.option: Runtime as the boundary, one VM per client
alternatives.why_not: Breaks on the first local project and on the first runtime hosting two clients.

alternatives.option: Per-project confidentiality settings
alternatives.why_not: With twelve projects you configure on autopilot, and the default decides instead of you.

decisions.title: The rules engine has no AI and reads only metadata
decisions.why: There is no global model reading everything because the global thing is not a model — so hallucination never enters the ranking of the user's attention.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: Enforced by construction rather than by a rule: `MetaEvent` has no variant that can hold content, so a leak is unrepresentable rather than forbidden. An import boundary keeping a model client out of `bancada-rules` would be a second, weaker guard on a door that has no opening. Recorded here so the guarantee is known to rest on the type, and would need a rule the day the type softens.

alternatives.option: An AI agent doing the triage
alternatives.why_not: Flexible, and it puts hallucination in the most dangerous possible place: the order of the attention queue.

alternatives.option: Rules only, no AI anywhere in the product
alternatives.why_not: Loses pre-digestion, which is half the value, and cannot distinguish "finished" from "only reported".

decisions.title: A file is not memory; only the product writes memory
decisions.why: Writing a file shows in a diff, passes review and reverts with git. Writing memory does none of those, and it is what the supervisor reads later.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: The distinction is between two writes to the same filesystem. Nothing in the import graph separates them.

alternatives.option: An MCP write channel straight into memory
alternatives.why_not: The record would feed itself, and unreviewed memory would accumulate generated content that degrades every future piece of advice.

alternatives.option: The supervisor writes memory, sessions do not
alternatives.why_not: The supervisor is AI as well. The distinction does not hold.

decisions.title: A plugin returns typed data, never DOM
decisions.why: A plugin loaded in the webview would see the channel to the core, which talks to every workspace — crossing every confidentiality boundary at once, through a mechanism the product introduced.

alternatives.option: HTML strings
alternatives.why_not: The previous contract. Stringly typed, no interactivity, and the theme guarantee depends on the plugin obeying documentation.

alternatives.option: A component in the host's framework
alternatives.why_not: Makes React a public API. Swapping it breaks every plugin, and version skew is a known trap.

alternatives.option: Web components
alternatives.why_not: Framework-agnostic and interactive, but shadow DOM isolates styles in both directions and it does not solve the sandbox.

decisions.title: The MCP server runs over stdio, as a child of the harness
decisions.why: No port, no network, no token: containment by construction rather than by policy.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: A transport choice lives in how a process is spawned, not in what any file imports.

alternatives.option: HTTP per workspace with an ephemeral token
alternatives.why_not: Easier to reach from any runtime — and *anything* in that runtime reaches the server, not just the agent. Containment by policy, not by construction.

alternatives.option: No MCP server at all, context injection only
alternatives.why_not: Injection serves what was anticipated; querying serves what was not.

decisions.title: Permission is a named profile, not a mode
decisions.why: A deny rule survives the most permissive base mode while an allow rule is inert under it, so the permissive mode you actually run can stay and still gate what is irreversible.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It describes the shape of a configuration the product reads, not the shape of the code that reads it.

alternatives.option: Permission mode per runtime
alternatives.why_not: Leaves the real gap: inside one runtime, irreversible infrastructure work and ordinary code get identical treatment.

alternatives.option: Mode chosen at session start
alternatives.why_not: Requires predicting what the session will touch. A tool-class policy catches it when it happens.

decisions.title: Computed reach between workspaces, not an abstract badge
decisions.why: A runtime boundary contains what is inside it and does not protect what is outside — one direction is guaranteed and the other is not, so an adjective would be a lie.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It is what the product computes and shows at runtime. No rule about source files can hold it.

alternatives.option: A hard / soft isolation badge
alternatives.why_not: Lies by omitting direction.

alternatives.option: Formal workspace types
alternatives.why_not: Resolves the symptom with a taxonomy; the computed fact resolves the cause.

decisions.title: Tauri shell, Rust core, React webview, bun for development
decisions.why: Everything reusable from prior work is presentation and everything new is systems work, so the split falls exactly where the toolchain boundary already is.

alternatives.option: Electron
alternatives.why_not: The weight lands exactly where this machine is already tight, and it would still end in a separate Node daemon.

alternatives.option: Wails, with Go
alternatives.why_not: Go is a better fit for the concurrent half and cross-compiles beautifully, but v3 is in alpha and v2 is the previous generation.

alternatives.option: Rust everywhere, WASM frontend
alternatives.why_not: Elegant, and it kills the plugin story: nobody writes a Rust plugin for a personal tool.

alternatives.option: Elixir and LiveView
alternatives.why_not: OTP supervises BEAM processes beautifully and OS processes awkwardly, and this product's core job is the second. LiveView also conflicts with a client-side plugin contract.

alternatives.option: Svelte instead of React
alternatives.why_not: Better shape fit for a live-updating queue, but the advantage is theoretical at 5–20 items, and mature editor tooling matters twice here.

alternatives.option: Business logic in the webview
alternatives.why_not: The seam has to stay one folder of commands somebody can read in a sitting, or the Rust core stops being the core.

decisions.title: Exact versions in every manifest, and bun is the only installer
decisions.why: A range says *some* version and a lockfile pins it for one checkout only, so a fresh `cargo add` or a deleted lockfile resolves differently and the difference shows up as a failure nobody edited into existence.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: The claim is about `package.json` and `Cargo.toml`, and archwarden reads source files rather than manifests. A rule shaped like this would be worth having; today the guard is review. Filed upstream as archwarden#177.

alternatives.option: Caret or tilde ranges, letting patches arrive on their own
alternatives.why_not: A patch that lands without anyone choosing it is also a patch nobody tested. Upgrades should be a commit with a name on them.

alternatives.option: npm alongside bun
alternatives.why_not: They write different lockfiles from one manifest, and a repository carrying both has two answers to "what version is this".

alternatives.option: Pinning the whole transitive graph by hand
alternatives.why_not: Fiction. The lockfile owns transitive versions; the pin is on direct dependencies.

decisions.title: The machine bancada runs on registers itself
decisions.why: The product is already executing there, so its prefix, path mapping and filesystem access are facts rather than claims — and asking a person to write them down is asking them to restate one.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It is behaviour at read time: a runtime synthesised before validation and dropped before writing. Nothing in the file layout shows it.

alternatives.option: Requiring the local machine to be registered like any other runtime
alternatives.why_not: Made the first five minutes absurd: describing your own laptop in JSON, every field of which the product could only have gotten right.

alternatives.option: Persisting the synthesised runtime into the configuration file
alternatives.why_not: Freezes today's `$HOME` into a file that outlives it, and the copy on disk quietly wins over the fact.

alternatives.option: A default that cannot be overridden
alternatives.why_not: A default that cannot be overridden is one that eventually lies. An entry somebody edited no longer equals the default and survives.

decisions.title: Warm paper, not a dark cockpit
decisions.why: A dark cockpit borrows its authority from instrument panels, and this is a place you read prose an agent wrote and decide whether you agree.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: The rule worth having — no colour literal outside `theme.css` — is neither a rendered element nor a callee, so no chokepoint reaches it. Filed upstream as archwarden#177.

alternatives.option: The dark instrument-panel palette
alternatives.why_not: Its principle held — colour is reserved for things that ask for an action — and its ground did not. Eight hours of reading on black feels like surveillance rather than work.

alternatives.option: Web fonts
alternatives.why_not: The app must open with no network at all, and a font that arrives late is a layout that moves under the reader.

alternatives.option: Monaco's stock themes
alternatives.why_not: Cold. A panel that does not belong to the page around it reads as a different program embedded in this one.

decisions.title: Five layers in the webview, enforced not agreed
decisions.why: The Rust side's boundaries are crates and a crate that imports what it may not does not compile; the webview had the same kinds of boundary and none of the enforcement.

alternatives.option: One flat components folder
alternatives.why_not: Worked at nine files and stopped at thirty. Pages reached into each other and the only thing keeping a component reusable was whoever last edited it remembering that it should be.

alternatives.option: Raw HTML wherever it is convenient
alternatives.why_not: A `<div className="flex gap-4">` in a page is a design decision made outside the design system. Consistency erodes one of those at a time, none wrong on its own.

alternatives.option: Plain CSS with custom properties, no Tailwind
alternatives.why_not: It is what the product had, and it worked. shadcn's components are written in utility classes, and rewriting each one by hand is a fork of upstream you then maintain forever. Tailwind is build-time only here, so nothing about the offline guarantee changes.

alternatives.option: Radix headless with hand-written CSS
alternatives.why_not: Considered and passed over: the palette was already tokens, but owning the component source is what lets archwarden govern it like anything else.

alternatives.option: Base UI, the MUI headless successor
alternatives.why_not: The API is still moving, which combines badly with a repository that pins exact versions and treats upgrades as deliberate commits.

alternatives.option: Writing every primitive ourselves, no dependency
alternatives.why_not: A correct modal is real work — focus trapped and restored, escape, scroll lock, aria — and getting it wrong is invisible until somebody uses a keyboard.

alternatives.option: Testing every view file
alternatives.why_not: Views are arrangement, and arrangement is checked by looking. Eleven standing warnings is how a real one gets missed.

decisions.title: A Rust file names what it exports
decisions.why: A type the product refers to by name should be findable by that name, and a file that hides one is a file you only find by grep.

alternatives.option: Any file may export anything
alternatives.why_not: Works until the crate has forty files, and then finding `SessionState` means grepping rather than looking.

decisions.title: Rust unit tests live inside the file they test
decisions.why: A test in the file can reach the private function it is testing, and moves with it when the file moves — which is the half no reviewer ever remembers to check.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: `spec-pair` looks for a sibling file, and an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` has none. The rule that claimed to keep this was deleted rather than fixed: a rule that cannot be written is better absent than dead and green. It also costs a clean coverage number — assertion machinery sits in the measured file — which is why the gate reads lcov rather than llvm-cov's own summary. Filed upstream as archwarden#178.

alternatives.option: A sibling spec file, the way the webview does it
alternatives.why_not: It cannot reach anything private, so it tests the crate's surface and calls it unit testing. The webview has sibling specs because TypeScript has no other option; Rust does.

alternatives.option: A separate `tests/` directory for everything
alternatives.why_not: That is where integration tests belong and they exist too — `app/src-tauri/tests` drives the commands against a real tree. A unit test put there stops being one the moment it can only see `pub` items.

decisions.title: The window is told, not asked
decisions.why: A screen that polls is stale for as long as its interval, and the interval is a guess about how impatient the reader is; watching the logs is exact, and it turns out to cost nothing because the logs are always a host path.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: Whether a screen listens or polls is behaviour. A rule can see that `setInterval` exists, not that it is a fallback rather than the mechanism — and the fallback is deliberate, so a rule forbidding the call would forbid the right code.

alternatives.option: Polling, on a short interval
alternatives.why_not: What shipped, at ten seconds, with `for now` written beside it. Every reader waits up to the interval for a change that already happened, and each poll runs `git diff` on every open project whether anything moved or not.

alternatives.option: `Runtime::watch`, so a runtime watches its own tree
alternatives.why_not: The architecture's hard rule 3 names it and it is not needed: `configDir` is written in this machine's spelling by definition — it is how the logs are read at all — so the logs of a VM, a container or an ssh host are already a local path. The harder problem was anticipated than the one that exists.

alternatives.option: An event carrying what changed
alternatives.why_not: A filesystem event says a line landed in some log, which is not a fact any screen is shaped around. A payload naming a path would invite a screen to believe it knows which of its questions went stale, and be wrong the first time two things moved at once.

alternatives.option: Falling back to polling in silence
alternatives.why_not: A window that looks live while it is a minute behind lies with more confidence than one that admits it. The same argument `RuntimeError::Unsupported` already makes about a watch that reports nothing.

decisions.title: A project can be told not to ask, and new work unmutes it
decisions.why: A project whose work has ended is noise in a queue whose whole value is that everything in it matters; but a silence you have to remember to lift is the exact forgetting an attention supervisor exists to prevent, so a session that did not exist when you silenced it wakes it on its own.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It is a claim about what reaches the queue. A rule can see that `Project::asking` exists, not that every screen counting what needs you goes through it — and the check that matters is that two screens agree, which is a property of two call sites rather than of a shape.

alternatives.option: A plain `active: bool`
alternatives.why_not: Silence that only a click can lift. You silence a project the day the work ends and start working there again three weeks later; the queue then says nothing about it, which is the one failure this product cannot have. Forgetting is what it is for.

alternatives.option: Unregister the project instead
alternatives.why_not: Loses the path, the workspace, the weight and the machine — everything you configured — to say "not this week". And re-registering is the long form, with a folder picker, for something that should be one click.

alternatives.option: Wake on any activity, using the log's modification time
alternatives.why_not: Available for free on both screens, and wrong: a conversation you already dismissed continuing is a write, so every silenced project would come back within minutes. The count of sessions distinguishes new work from work you already declined to look at.

alternatives.option: Wake on a session whose first event is after the silencing
alternatives.why_not: The exact rule, and it needs the *content* of every log to find the first event. The work list deliberately reads no content — it costs a process per project per open — so this rule would be computable on one screen and not the other, and two screens deciding "is this asking for me" two ways is how a product disagrees with itself about what needs you.

alternatives.option: Stop reading a silenced project altogether
alternatives.why_not: Cheaper, and it makes the waking rule impossible: nothing would notice the new session. It also hides the project from the screen where you would go to bring it back.

decisions.title: A newer session quiets the ones that had already stopped
decisions.why: A session you walked away from stays `awaiting_human` forever — nothing clears it but a next event, and the score multiplies by age, so it grew louder every minute until it outranked the session you were actually in; starting the next session is the signal you have moved on, and it costs nobody a button they would forget to press.
decisions.why_not_enforceable: It is a claim about which rows reach the queue. A rule can see that `SessionState::queue` exists, not that every caller hands it a whole project rather than one log — and handing it one log is exactly the mistake, because it type-checks, passes, and silently disables the rule.

alternatives.option: Leave it: a finished turn asks until you answer it
alternatives.why_not: What shipped, and the bug. Nothing clears `awaiting_human` but a next event, an abandoned session has none, and age multiplies the score — so the session you walked away from yesterday outranks the one you are in now, and a queue with rows you have learned to skip is a queue you stop reading.

alternatives.option: Silence one session by hand, the way a project is silenced
alternatives.why_not: ADR-023's shape at session granularity, and it needs you to remember at the one moment you are not thinking about the supervisor: walking away. A silence that only a click can lift is the failure ADR-023 is itself written against. It survives inverted, as `kept` — you name the few you hold, not the many you abandon.

alternatives.option: Expire a finished turn after a fixed time
alternatives.why_not: A ceiling to match the floor `idleAfterMinutes` already is. It is a silence nobody asked for, set by a number chosen by hand, and it drops rows with no signal that it was about to — where a newer session is a fact you produced yourself.

alternatives.option: Cap the age factor so an old row cannot outrank a live one
alternatives.why_not: Treats the ordering and leaves the row. Worth having on its own merits, and it does not answer the question, which is that the session is over rather than merely old.

alternatives.option: Only the single newest session may ask
alternatives.why_not: The simplest version, and wrong for the product: running several agents at once is the case this exists for, and it would quiet the parallel session that is still working. Comparing each session's own last activity against the newest one's first event costs nothing and keeps them.

alternatives.option: Quiet a raised decision too, for consistency
alternatives.why_not: An agent stopped on a question cannot continue at all. It is the row it would be worst to lose, and losing it to a rule about tidiness is the one trade nothing here justifies.

rules.why: The webview and the core are joined by a string that no import records and no resolver can see. It is the one boundary in this repository that neither cargo nor tsc can check, which is exactly why it is here.
A #[tauri::command] is the surface the webview can reach. Keeping them in one folder is what makes reviewing that surface something a person can do in one sitting.
Barrels are exempt by construction, so this asks only of files that declare something of their own.

A plugin returns typed data and never touches the DOM or the channel to the core. Reaching host internals is how a plugin would cross every workspace boundary at once, through a mechanism we introduced. ADR-006.
Five layers and no sixth. A folder that is not one of these is a place the import rules do not reach, and an ungoverned folder becomes the one everything ends up in.
A component that has heard of a queue or a project can only be used once. The alphabet has to stay an alphabet.
The frame says how things sit, never what they are. A Stack that imports a Button has stopped being spacing and become a component.
A composite knows how its parts fit together and still knows nothing about the product. Reaching up to a layout or a page would make it un-reusable, which is the one thing it exists to be.
A layout takes children and arranges them; it never knows what they are, and never goes looking for them. That is what lets the cockpit and the review share one shell.
Pages are the only layer that is not reusable. Anything importing one is trying to reuse it, and what it wants belongs in a lower layer or in `pages/_shared`.
`core` is what the Rust side hands over and the pure functions over it. A core module that imports a component has put rendering behind the seam, where no test can see it.

Raw HTML in a layout or a page is a design decision made outside the design system, and consistency erodes one `<div className=...>` at a time — none of them wrong on their own. Everything above `components` and `frame` composes from what is already there, or adds to it.
A component rendered by name must be findable by name. It is also what keeps a plugin contribution and a host component out of one namespace.

An error, not a warning, because it is scoped to the files that hold reasoning: the seam to Rust and each page's `logic`. Views are arrangement, and arrangement is checked by looking — a rule that warned about every one of them would be eleven warnings nobody reads, which is how a real one gets missed.
